Standard deposit 20% Cancellation cut-off 48 hours Pricing currency IDR Package Credit Non-expiring · one transfer Policy Policy Hub Booking, Payment & Cancellation Inclusions & Exclusions Privacy & Data Protection Browse tours How booking works Website-only booking. JVTO accepts bookings exclusively through the official website checkout under a valid JVTO Booking ID. WhatsApp/email are support channels only — they never create, confirm, modify, cancel, or transfer a booking. Deposit & payment Standard deposit : 20% of total booking value (card via secure JVTO link) Close-departure rule : if Day 1 is within 14 days, JVTO may require up to 100% full payment Card balance deadline : no later than 5 days before Day 1 Bank wire / Wise balance deadline : no later than 3 days before Day 1 Cash at JVTO office : only if approved in writing in advance Lifetime Package Guarantee — the rules in plain language Lifetime Package Guarantee Your confirmed package does not disappear when plans change early. Cancel your entire booking at least 48 hours before Day 1 and the same package, your original number of travellers, and your original confirmed package price remain available for future use as Lifetime Package Credit. Cancel your booking 48h+ before Day 1 Cancel the complete booking 48 hours or more before Day 1: you receive Lifetime Package Credit. It never expires and preserves the same package, original pax entitlement, and original confirmed price, and can be transferred once. Package Credit is not cash and cannot be exchanged for cash. Cancel within 48h of Day 1 Cancel the complete booking less than 48 hours before Day 1: the booking is forfeited and no Package Credit is created. One traveller cancels (booking continues) If one or more travellers cancel but the tour continues, the cancelled travellers receive a cash refund of their confirmed price: 100% at 48 hours or more before Day 1, 50% within 48 hours, and 0% after Day 1. At least 2 paying travellers must remain, otherwise it is treated as a full cancellation. Flight disruption If a verified natural transport disruption (for example volcanic ash) cancels your flight, your package can be reactivated once for a 50% Recovery Fee of the original confirmed package price. Destination force majeure If a verified official event affects your destination and the whole tour is impossible, you can choose Lifetime Package Credit or a cash refund less any non-recoverable vendor cost. If only part is affected, JVTO first offers an alternative route, then a refund of the affected component. Transferring Package Credit Package Credit may be transferred once to another person. The old credit code is closed and a new one is issued to the recipient. A second transfer is not permitted. Using Package Credit To use Package Credit, choose a new date for the same package. Your original pax entitlement appears automatically; fewer travellers yields no refund, and more travellers are charged the incremental website price. The best month depends on which destination is your priority — there is no single perfect season for all three at once. The short answer: dry season (May–October) gives the clearest Bromo sunrises and safest Ijen night hikes. Wet season (November–April) peaks Tumpak Sewu waterfall volume. May and September hit the sweet spot — dry conditions with fewer crowds than July–August peak. Dry Season May – October ✓ Clearest Bromo sunrises ✓ Best Ijen blue fire visibility ✓ Drier, safer Tumpak Sewu trail ✗ July–Aug peak crowds — book 3–4 weeks ahead Wet Season November – April ✓ Tumpak Sewu at maximum volume ✓ Lowest crowds and best accommodation rates ✗ Cloudier Bromo dawns (still possible) ✗ Slippery trail descent at Tumpak Sewu Month-by-Month Quick Reference Month Bromo Sunrise Ijen Blue Fire Tumpak Sewu Crowds January Variable Accessible Peak Low February Variable Accessible Peak Low March Improving Good Excellent Low April Good Good Excellent Low May ★ Excellent Excellent Good Medium June Excellent Excellent Good Medium July Excellent Excellent Good High August Excellent Excellent Good High September ★ Excellent Excellent Good Medium October Good Good Good Low November Variable Variable Building Low December Variable Accessible Building Low ★ sweet-spot months — best dry-season conditions with below-peak crowds Per-Destination Breakdown Mount Bromo The classic Bromo sunrise requires cloud-free skies at Penanjakan viewpoint (2,770 m) at around 05:00 AM. This is most reliable May through September , when dry south-east trade winds clear the caldera overnight. July and August have the best weather reliability but also the highest visitor numbers — expect 50+ jeeps at the viewpoint in peak months. The April and October shoulder months offer nearly identical conditions with noticeably fewer tourists and lower jeep rates. In the wet season (November–March), clear mornings still occur — roughly 50–60% of departures based on JVTO operational records. We monitor BMKG forecasts the evening before each tour. Ijen Crater & Blue Fire Ijen blue fire — burning sulfur gases at the active crater lake — is visible year-round on JVTO night hikes. The seasonal difference is visibility inside the crater: May to October provides the lowest humidity and clearest conditions for photographing blue flames. Pre-dawn temperatures at the crater rim drop to 5–8°C in July–August — bring a warm jacket regardless of departure month. JVTO includes a gas mask for all Ijen guests as standard. Sulfur gas is a daily operational reality regardless of season — our guides monitor PVMBG volcanic activity levels before each tour. See: Ijen Health Screening (SE.1658 protocol) . Tumpak Sewu Waterfall Tumpak Sewu is genuinely more spectacular in the wet season. January through April brings peak water volume — the curtain of 120+ individual falls is at its widest and most powerful. If maximum waterfall impact is your goal, plan for this window. The trade-off is that the 1.5 km descent trail through Glidih Canyon becomes slippery, with rope-assisted sections requiring care. From May to October , the trail is drier and safer. The waterfall flow remains impressive (rivers are fed by mountain springs, not only rain). JVTO guides carry the necessary ropes and assess trail safety on arrival before starting the descent. JVTO Operating Notes We operate year-round. Rainy season is not an automatic cancellation trigger. We make go/no-go decisions based on real-time BMKG (weather) and PVMBG (volcanic activity) data the evening before each tour. Weather risk is covered by Package Credit. If a tour must be modified or cut short due to weather or volcanic closure, guests receive JVTO Package Credit (non-expiring) for the affected portion. Read: Weather & Closures policy . Peak season booking advice. For July and August departures, book at least 3–4 weeks in advance. Accommodation in the Tengger Caldera area and Banyuwangi fills quickly during European summer holidays and Indonesian National Day week. Browse private tour packages → ◆ Quick Answers Seasonal Planning: Common Questions What is the best time to visit Mount Bromo? May through September (dry season) is the best time for Mount Bromo. Clear skies at dawn produce the iconic sea-of-clouds sunrise over the Tengger Caldera. July and August are the peak months but attract the largest crowds. April and October offer nearly identical conditions with fewer visitors and lower accommodation rates. When can you see the Ijen blue fire? Ijen blue fire is visible year-round during JVTO night hikes, but May to October offers the clearest sightlines — lower humidity, less cloud cover inside the crater, and drier trail conditions on the descent to the sulfur lake. Blue flames from burning sulfur gases appear most vivid between midnight and 03:00 AM regardless of month. JVTO night hikes depart at around 00:00–01:00 AM to reach the crater by the peak blue-fire window. Is Tumpak Sewu waterfall better in wet season or dry season? Tumpak Sewu is most impressive in the wet season (January–April) when waterfall volume peaks after sustained rainfall. The curtain of 120+ individual falls is at its widest and most powerful during this period. However, the descent trail through Glidih Canyon becomes slippery and rope-assisted sections require care. The dry season (May–October) offers safer, drier footing with still-impressive flow. JVTO guides assess trail conditions on arrival before starting the descent. What months make up the rainy season in East Java? East Java's rainy season typically runs from November through March, with December and January being the wettest months. Rain usually falls as heavy afternoon and evening showers rather than continuous drizzle, so morning tours to Bromo and Ijen are still viable. Tours are not automatically cancelled in the rainy season — JVTO monitors BMKG and PVMBG forecasts before each departure and decides based on real conditions. What is the peak tourist season in East Java? Peak season is July and August, coinciding with European summer school holidays and Indonesian National Day (17 August). Bromo sunrise viewpoints at Penanjakan are significantly busier, and accommodation in the Tengger Caldera area books out quickly. JVTO private tours operate normally during peak season, but we recommend booking at least 3–4 weeks ahead for July–August departures. What is the coldest month at Ijen Crater? July and August are the coldest months at Ijen Crater. Pre-dawn temperatures at the crater rim (2,386 m) can drop to 5–8°C, and the descent to the sulfur lake adds wind-chill exposure. JVTO provides a gas mask for all guests as standard. Guests should bring a warm jacket, gloves, and a wind layer — especially for July–August night hikes. Is December a good time to visit Bromo? December marks the start of the rainy season and cloud cover at dawn is more frequent than in dry season. Sunrise conditions are less predictable — roughly 40–50% of departures in December–January encounter partial or full cloud cover at the Penanjakan viewpoint. JVTO monitors BMKG the evening before every tour and advises guests when forecasts look poor. A clear December sunrise is still possible; it is simply less guaranteed than May–September. What is the best single month to visit all three destinations? May or September offer the best combination: dry-season conditions for Bromo and Ijen, decent Tumpak Sewu flow (not peak, but still strong), and significantly fewer crowds than July–August. May and September also tend to have lower accommodation rates. If Tumpak Sewu waterfall volume is your priority over everything else, March or April (late wet season) is the better choice — but expect wet trail conditions and pack accordingly. The full legal text is at javavolcano-touroperator.com/policy/booking-payment-cancellation . What follows is the practical summary. How to Book Bookings are made only on the official JVTO website (javavolcano-touroperator.com). It is a five-step process: Choose your route and dates — browse packages on the website and select your date, origin (Surabaya or Bali), group size, and route. Receive your Official E-Voucher — a PDF is issued after deposit payment. This is your booking reference and includes your full trip details and pre-trip guide. Access My Booking Portal — post-payment, you gain access to your personal booking dashboard using your lead traveller email. WhatsApp (+62 822 4478 8833) and email are support-only channels — they help you plan and answer questions before and during the tour, but they never create, confirm, modify, cancel, or transfer a booking. Booking is confirmed only when: (1) a package has been selected, (2) the required payment has been processed, and (3) the Official E-Voucher / Invoice (PDF) has been issued by JVTO. Book With a Licensed, Verifiable Operator Not every business advertising East Java volcano trips is a registered tour operator. This matters because unlicensed operators are a documented, police-charged fraud risk in East Java — a category-level risk, not a claim about any particular company. In one case reported by the Indonesian National Police, the owner of an unlicensed ("bodong") Banyuwangi travel agency was arrested over a fake overseas-tour scheme: around 18 travellers each paid roughly 10 million rupiah for tours that never ran, and police said the packages were "merely his cover to get money." He was charged with fraud and embezzlement under the Indonesian Criminal Code (Polres Sukoharjo, Indonesian National Police, 2019). Separately — and as an unrelated matter of ordinary crime rather than operator conduct — travellers in the region face the everyday theft risk present at any destination, which is why dealing with accountable, identifiable people matters. Police, for example, investigated the theft of foreign tourists' luggage from a vehicle near Mount Bromo in early 2026; the local police chief noted the incident "affects the image of Mount Bromo as a safe destination" and pledged professional handling (ANTARA News, 2026). JVTO is the opposite of an anonymous, website-only operator. PT Java Volcano Rendezvous is a licensed business you can check for yourself: national business registration NIB 1102230032918, a TDUP tourism business permit, HPWKI (Himpunan Pelaku Wisata Khusus Ijen) operator membership, and BBKSDA conservation-area compliance. It has operated in East Java since 2015 and is founder-led by an active Indonesian Tourist Police officer. It also works from a physical office in Bondowoso — Jl. Khairil Anwar No.102A, East Java 68214 — a real, fixed address you can locate, not just a web page. Booking is handled on the record through the official JVTO website, but behind that website stands a registered company with a permanent office you can verify — unlike an operator that exists only as a website or social-media account, with no traceable licence, no office, and no one to hold accountable. The people who run your tour are just as verifiable. JVTO relies on a permanent, named crew — not freelancers assembled for each booking . Its Ijen guides and drivers are registered HPWKI members who carry individual KTA membership credentials issued by the association, and each active crew member is listed by name on the JVTO team page. HPWKI is not an informal label: it is a legally established association registered with the Ministry of Law (AHU/SABH), and JVTO's founder, Agung Sambuko, is named among its governing officers — serving as a pengawas (supervisory-board member). That places JVTO inside the crater's regulated guiding system rather than outside it — a system overseen by BBKSDA Jawa Timur, the conservation authority for Kawah Ijen, which conducts formal guide training for the site (BBKSDA Jawa Timur / KSDAE, "Pelatihan Pemandu Kawah Ijen," 29 May 2024). When the company, its office, and every guide are registered and named, someone is accountable at every step of your trip — the baseline protection that an unverifiable "bodong" operator, which may be nothing more than a website, cannot offer. The named people behind JVTO are just as checkable, and its track record is externally recognised. Founder Agung Sambuko is an active officer in Bondowoso's Tourism Police (Ditpamobvit, East Java) — the unit set up to support the Ijen Geopark — a role documented in national press and backed by police service orders, not just a bio line. The mandatory Ijen health screening is coordinated by Dr. Ahmad Irwandanu , a licensed general practitioner whose medical registration (STR QN00001073380217, valid to 2031-01-06) is publicly checkable through the Ministry of Health's SatuSehat and KKI registries. JVTO's history also predates the company: the founder's guesthouse earned a Booking.com Guest Review Award in 2015 (score 9.4/10, "Ijen Bondowoso Home Stay," shipped to the same Bondowoso address JVTO uses today) and appears in the German guidebook Stefan Loose Reiseführer Indonesien (ISBN 9783770167654, page 287). Cash balance at the JVTO office : a cash (IDR) balance may be settled in person at the JVTO office when you arrive, before Day 1, only if approved in writing in advance — and only if you have already converted your money to IDR yourself. JVTO does not exchange currency, does not recommend or partner with any money changer, and cannot guarantee exchange rates. All pricing is in IDR. Prices are quoted and invoiced in Indonesian Rupiah. This scheme is not available through third-party platforms (GetYourGuide, Booking.com, etc.). My Booking Portal After payment, the lead traveller gains access to My Booking Portal using the email address provided at booking. The portal is your live record of the trip and your task management tool for the pre-tour checklist. What the portal shows: Tour dates and package summary Pick-up details and vehicle/crew assignment Accommodation plan Daily itinerary Notes from JVTO E-Voucher download link What the portal lets you do: Submit your guest list Confirm pick-up and drop-off addresses Set rooming preferences Note dietary requirements Complete your pre-trip to-do checklist Access My Booking Portal at javavolcano-touroperator.com using your lead traveller email. Your E-Voucher — The Booking Reference The Official E-Voucher (PDF) is issued after deposit payment. It is your primary booking reference. Keep it accessible throughout your trip — digital on your phone is sufficient for most checkpoints; a paper passport may be required at crater-access gates. The E-Voucher shows: tour dates, package inclusions, pick-up time and location, contact details for WhatsApp and email, and payment status. In all disputes, the E-Voucher takes precedence over verbal confirmations or informal messages. Check it when it arrives and flag any discrepancies to JVTO immediately. Amendments and Reschedules One free reschedule is available if requested 48 hours or more before Day 1, subject to availability. Reschedules requested less than 48 hours before Day 1 are not permitted. Significant route changes that alter the primary destination sequence are not available — JVTO does not offer unbundled or transport-only services. Cancellation and Package Credit Full cancellation: ≥ 48 hours before Day 1 : 100% converts to Lifetime Package Credit — never cash. Non-expiring; locked to the same package, traveler count and price; cannot be split or changed to another package; transferable to another person once, with written authorisation. < 48 hours before Day 1, or a no-show : booking forfeited up to 100%; no Package Credit is issued. Partial cancellation (some travelers drop while at least two paying travelers remain) — cash refund on the cancelled seats only: 100% if ≥ 48 hours before Day 1, 50% if < 48 hours, 0% once the tour has started. Dropping below two paying travelers is treated as a full cancellation. Flight disruption — if a confirmed flight is cancelled or rescheduled by the airline and no alternative works, JVTO applies a 50% flight Recovery Fee and converts the remainder to Lifetime Package Credit. Cash refunds are not available for a full guest-initiated cancellation. For closures caused by volcanic activity, government restrictions, or force majeure, JVTO may offer Package Credit, alternatives, or partial cash refunds — assessed per situation. Tap any question to expand. If yours is not here, ask via WhatsApp — a human answers, 08:00–22:00 WIB. A · Tours & Booking Basics Are your tours private or shared? All JVTO tours are private only. We do not mix your booking with other guests or sell “seat in coach” options. Your vehicle, driver and guide are arranged for your party alone. For examples of private itineraries from Surabaya or Bali, see our Tours pages. What is included in the price? Each tour page shows a clear list of Inclusions and Exclusions. In general, our private, all-inclusive packages cover: Private vehicle and driver Bromo 4WD jeep where listed Stated park entrance tickets and permits All hotel breakfasts Selected lunches and dinners (especially during the Bondowoso / Ijen segment) Mineral water Essential gear for Ijen (gas mask and trekking pole) on tours that include Ijen JVTO travel T-shirt (where listed) Anything not listed under “Included” is treated as not included. For full details, please see Booking Information and the Inclusions & Exclusions section of your chosen tour. How do I book and confirm a tour? The usual steps are: You send us your dates, origin (for example Surabaya or Bali), group size and preferred route. We send you a tailored proposal with itinerary and price. You confirm in writing and pay the booking deposit (normally 20% of the total). We send you an official JVTO E-Voucher with your booking details. Your booking is considered confirmed when the deposit has been received and the E-Voucher has been issued. Full details are on the Booking Information page. How do payments, deposits and deadlines work? In most cases: A deposit is required to secure your booking. The remaining balance is due a few days before Day 1 of your tour, depending on the payment method (for example card vs bank transfer). If payment deadlines are missed, your booking may be at risk. The exact amounts and dates are always stated in your E-Voucher and explained on our Booking Information page. That page and your E-Voucher together act as the official reference. What is Package Credit and do you offer cash refunds? JVTO uses a Package Credit system instead of standard cash refunds for most guest-initiated cancellations. In general: If you cancel far enough in advance (before the stated cutoff), we convert your paid amounts into Package Credit. Package Credit can be used for future JVTO tours, and may be transferable under the rules stated in our policy. Package Credit does not normally expire. Cash refunds are not normally provided except in specially defined situations. Exact timing thresholds, percentages and special cases are described in detail on the Booking Information page and in the Booking & Cancellation Policy. B · Safety, Health & Insurance How does the Ijen health screening work? For tours that include the Ijen night hike, JVTO includes a mandatory health screening run by approved medical staff. The aim is to reduce the risk of sending unfit guests into a demanding environment with sulphur gas and steep trails. Key points: Screening takes place before the hike, often at your accommodation or a partner clinic. Basic checks are done (for example blood pressure, oxygen saturation and relevant medical history). Results are recorded and can be used to confirm whether the hike is appropriate. The certificate is BSrE (Balai Sertifikasi Elektronik / BSSN) electronically signed and traceable to the licensed doctor's SIP, which helps prevent fake or self-issued certificates. Full details, including what happens if you are not cleared, are explained on Ijen Health Screening. What happens if I do not pass the Ijen health screening? If screening staff or our team advise that you should not attempt the hike, we will follow that decision. It is made to protect your safety and others on the trail. In these cases, we may: Offer alternative low-risk activities or rest time, where practical Continue the rest of your itinerary as planned Financial treatment (for example how costs for the Ijen segment are handled) follows the rules set in our Booking Information and policy. Do I need travel insurance? Yes, we strongly recommend that all guests hold valid travel insurance that covers: Medical emergencies Evacuation and repatriation Trip interruption and cancellations JVTO operates as a licensed Indonesian tour operator, but we cannot act as an insurance provider and cannot cover costs that fall under personal insurance. Can children or older travellers join JVTO tours? Many families and older travellers have joined our tours safely and comfortably. The key is matching itinerary difficulty to the real fitness and health of the guests: Some routes (for example Tumpak Sewu and the full Ijen hike) are physically demanding. Others can be adapted with more viewpoints and less intense trails. Please tell us clearly about ages and relevant conditions when you first contact us. We may suggest a slower or gentler plan based on your group’s needs. What if I feel unwell during the tour? Tell your driver or guide as soon as you notice it – do not wait until it becomes an emergency. Because your tour is private, we have more flexibility to: Adjust the pace Add extra rest stops Change or skip certain activities when it is safer to do so For serious symptoms, we will prioritise getting you to appropriate medical support. Always follow the instructions of your crew in such situations. C · Weather, Volcano Alerts & Closures What happens if Bromo or Ijen is closed on my dates? We follow official instructions from Indonesian authorities and park management. Depending on the situation: We may adjust timings or use alternative viewpoints We may replace certain stops with other available local visits In more serious cases, specific segments (such as a night hike) may be cancelled while other parts of the tour continue How this affects your booking financially is explained in the Weather & Closures and Booking Information pages. External closures are handled differently from voluntary cancellations. Will I definitely see sunrise views or the blue fire? No. Weather, cloud, volcanic gas and other natural factors are outside our control. We design our itineraries to maximise the chance of good conditions We cannot promise specific colours, light or blue fire visibility on any given night Our commitment is to honest briefings and to acting quickly if conditions become unsafe. If it rains, will our tour be cancelled? Light or normal rain rarely cancels an entire tour, but it can: Make trails more slippery Reduce visibility Require changes in timing or route Severe weather, landslides or dangerous conditions can lead to partial or full cancellations for safety. Our Weather & Closures page explains how we respond and how this links to Package Credit and itinerary changes. D · Luggage, Packing & Practicalities How much luggage can I bring? In most cases, standard airline-style luggage is fine: One main suitcase or backpack per person One small daypack If you plan to travel with unusually large or heavy items, please tell us in advance so we can plan the right vehicle. On days with hikes, we recommend leaving your main luggage in the car or accommodation and carrying only what you need in a daypack. What should I wear and bring for these tours? The key is layering, grip and simplicity: Layered clothing for cold pre-dawn starts and warmer later hours Closed shoes with good grip (hiking shoes recommended for Ijen and Tumpak Sewu) Small backpack, personal headlamp or torch, waterproof cover for electronics Essential personal medication We recommend keeping non-essential valuables and jewellery to a minimum, and avoiding silver items during Ijen days due to sulphur. E · Students, Groups & Police Escort Do you offer ISIC student deals? Yes. Through our collaboration with ISIC, verified international students may access adapted rates on selected packages. The goal is to keep travel fair for students facing higher foreign entrance fees, without reducing safety or quality. The exact conditions and eligible tours are explained on our ISIC / Student Deals page. Can you arrange an official police escort for our group? For large groups (typically around 18 guests or more), JVTO can help coordinate an official traffic police escort on certain road segments (for example from a toll exit to Bondowoso), if approved by the relevant Traffic Police unit. Key points: Escorts are based on formal written orders from the authorities Routes and times are clearly defined The aim is safe convoy management, not speeding or bypassing laws This is not automatic and not a marketing gimmick. Full details are on Police Escort for Groups. F · Communication & Support How can we contact JVTO before and during the tour? Before and during your tour, our official channels are: WhatsApp (primary) Email These details appear on your E-Voucher and on the Contact page. text: Ijen Health Screening – Real Checks, Digital Proof & BSrE Signature | JVTO Skip to main content Tourist Police-Led Private Tours | Licensed East Java Operator (No. 1102230032918) Tours Popular 3 Day Bromo, Madakaripura & Ijen 3 Day Ijen, Bromo, Madakaripura 4 Day Ijen, Bromo, Madakaripura By Location Start From Surabaya Start From Bali All Tours 16 private itineraries · Surabaya & Bali Destinations Why JVTO Travel Guide Home › Travel Guide › Ijen Health Screening Mandatory · BBKSDA SE.1658 GUIDE / IJEN-HEALTH Ijen health-screening coordination. A health certificate is mandatory for every guest before Kawah Ijen crater entry under BBKSDA rules. JVTO coordinates the check with a named, licensed physician — and the certificate is a BSrE-signed digital document, not a souvenir letter. Regulatory basis BBKSDA SE.1658/KSA.9/2024 Physician Dr. Ahmad Irwandanu · SIP Where Your hotel, the evening before Certificate BSrE-signed, checked at the gate Travel Guide Guide overview Ijen Health Screening Packing & Fitness Weather & Closures Safety on Tours Booking Information Police Escort for Groups FAQ Browse tours Reading time · 6 min · Medical reference What the Access Rule Is BBKSDA Jawa Timur — the government conservation agency responsible for the Kawah Ijen Natural Tourism Park — issued Surat Edaran SE.1658/KSA.9/2024 establishing health-certificate requirements for Ijen crater zone access. A health certificate is mandatory for every guest before Kawah Ijen crater entry, per BBKSDA SE.1658/KSA.9/2024. JVTO coordinates the mandatory clinic workflow under this regulation. The certificate requirement is regulatory, set by BBKSDA East Java. It is not unilaterally imposed by JVTO — BBKSDA sets the rule; JVTO coordinates the workflow so every crater-zone guest can satisfy it. At the crater access gate, checkpoint staff check the certificate. No valid health certificate means no crater-zone access. Why the Screening Is Real — and Why That Matters The Kawah Ijen ascent is genuinely demanding, and the authorities have attributed multiple visitor deaths on the trail to exhaustion and pre-existing conditions — a 49-year-old visitor from Bogor in 2015, a 64-year-old visitor from Jakarta in 2023, and a 53-year-old Polish visitor in 2024, each of whom collapsed on the climb ( detikNews, 2015 ; detikJatim, 2023 ; kumparan, 2024 ). It is a steep, gas-exposed route with limited evacuation options, and physical fitness genuinely matters. That is why BBKSDA Jawa Timur has, since January 2024, required a doctor-issued health certificate (surat keterangan sehat) for every Kawah Ijen visitor — to keep people who are unwell or who have conditions such as asthma or heart disease from being cleared to force the ascent ( TIMES Indonesia, 2024 ; Liputan6, 2024 ). But a certificate only protects anyone if the screening behind it is real. Within weeks of the rule, authorities found counterfeit surat sehat in circulation: BBKSDA and TWA Ijen ticket-counter staff flagged two forged certificates, and the Banyuwangi Health Office (Dinkes) confirmed the doctor signatures were not genuine. The forgeries were traced to a former employee of Puskesmas Kabat, who had scanned a doctor's signature onto certificates carrying the clinic's letterhead; the Health Office responded with a circular barring any certificate issued without a genuine medical examination ( Liputan6, 2024 ; Kabar Banyuwangi, 2024 ; BWI24JAM, 2024 ). JVTO's screening is the real thing. It is an actual examination by a named, SIP-licensed doctor — Dr. Ahmad Irwandanu — that produces a genuine certificate, not a scanned signature or a purchased form. The certificate is signed with a BSrE (Balai Sertifikasi Elektronik / BSSN) electronic signature — Indonesia's national electronic-certification standard, legally valid under UU ITE — so it is a recorded, licensed, tamper-evident document traceable to the licensed doctor who issued it. JVTO makes no claim about what the Ijen ticket gate does or does not verify — the point is simply that the screening behind the certificate is genuinely carried out by a medical professional, not self-issued or purchased. The screening is included in the package and carried out at your hotel before departure. That is exactly the safeguard the BBKSDA rule exists to protect: no valid health certificate, no crater access. Sources detikNews (2015) — visitor death on the Gunung Ijen ascent: https://news.detik.com/berita-jawa-timur/d-3040438/lagi-wisatawan-asal-bogor-meninggal-saat-mendaki-gunung-ijen detikJatim (2023) — visitor death after the Kawah Ijen climb: https://www.detik.com/jatim/wisata/d-7116796/wisatawan-asal-jakarta-meninggal-usai-daki-kawah-ijen-banyuwangi kumparan (2024) — visitor death on the Kawah Ijen ascent: https://kumparan.com/kumparannews/turis-asal-polandia-tewas-saat-mendaki-kawah-ijen-diduga-kelelahan-22B6m8T4WRj TIMES Indonesia (2024) — Kawah Ijen visitors required to carry a health certificate: https://banyuwangi.times.co.id/news/peristiwa/e1oqyrujmv/pengunjung-kawah-ijen-wajib-bawa-surat-keterangan-sehat Portal Kabar Banyuwangi (2024) — counterfeit health certificates used to enter TWA Ijen: https://kabarbanyuwangi.co.id/suket-sehat-diduga-abalabal-beredar-digunakan-wisatawan-masuk-ke-twa-ijen Liputan6 (2024) — forged Ijen health certificate traced to a former Puskesmas Kabat employee: https://www.liputan6.com/surabaya/read/5510716/terkuak-pemalsu-surat-sehat-ke-kawah-ijen-adalah-mantan-pegawai-puskesmas-kabat-banyuwangi BWI24JAM (2024) — Dinkes Banyuwangi warning after suspected certificate forgery: https://bwi24jam.co.id/temukan-dugaan-pemalsuan-sks-untuk-mendaki-kawah-ijen-dinkes-banyuwangi-beri-peringatan What the Screening Checks The health screening is conducted by licensed medical staff. Vitals measured include: SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation) Blood pressure Heart rate Respiratory history Results are recorded digitally on a BSrE-signed certificate. The BSrE (Balai Sertifikasi Elektronik / BSSN) electronic signature — a legally valid e-signature under UU ITE, traceable to the doctor's SIP — makes the certificate accountable and tamper-evident, a safeguard against a forged or self-issued paper copy. A valid certificate is checked at the crater access gate. The same screening is available beyond JVTO guests: participating clinics and hotels in the Ijen area can provide it to non-JVTO travellers. This is not a competitive restriction — it raises the safety standard for all visitors. The Process — How JVTO Coordinates It For every guest on an Ijen crater route, JVTO arranges the following mandatory sequence via the Ijen Digital Health Security System ( https://health.mountijen.com ): The nurse visits your hotel the evening before the Ijen hike — in the Bondowoso or Banyuwangi area. Vitals are checked at your accommodation. No travel to a clinic is required. The BSrE-signed digital certificate is issued for cleared guests. At the Paltuding trailhead , BBKSDA checkpoint staff check the certificate before permitting crater-zone access. The entire session takes place at your hotel before departure, not on the trail. Where screening takes place Screening can be arranged at three locations depending on your itinerary: Facility Location Type Klinik Bakti Husada Bondowoso Certified medical clinic (Kemenkes RI) — physical clinic Puskesmas Licin Banyuwangi Government health centre (Dinkes Banyuwangi) Hotel / JVTO office session Your accommodation Mobile session by Dr. Irwandanu before departure The Doctor — Verifiable Credentials Health-screening coordination at JVTO uses licensed medical staff. The supervising physician is Dr. Ahmad Irwandanu , holding a valid SIP (Surat Izin Praktik) issued by the Indonesian Ministry of Health (Kemenkes RI). Dr. Irwandanu's SIP is publicly verifiable at: satusehat.kemkes.go.id/sdmk Screening is performed by a credentialed provider under an active government-issued licence — not a formality or a self-certification by JVTO. What Happens If You Are Not Cleared to Hike If screening staff or the JVTO team advise that you should not attempt the Ijen hike, that decision is followed. The climb is cancelled for that individual, not the group. Alternatives include waiting at base camp or a safe viewpoint area at Paltuding. The screening session cost is non-refundable. The rest of the group continues. This outcome protects the individual guest and other guests on the trail. The screening is not a barrier to tourism — it is a check that prevents sending a guest with an undetected condition into a demanding environment with sulphur gas, steep terrain, and limited evacuation options. Screening Does Not Guarantee a Safe Hike Health-certificate screening is a pre-hike assessment, not a guarantee. Conditions on the mountain can still change after screening is completed. JVTO may still cancel the hike after screening if volcanic gas, weather, or BBKSDA closures make the route unsafe. The certificate is a mandatory condition of access — it does not remove the operational risks of an active volcano environment. Guests with heart, lung, or circulation conditions are advised to consult their own doctor before booking, in addition to the mandatory pre-hike screening. Screening Photos Evidence of the actual screening process conducted at hotels and the JVTO office: Scene Image Blood pressure check at hotel lobby https://javavolcano-touroperator.com/screening/ijen-screening-hotel-01.jpeg Vitals recorded at hotel table before night ascent https://javavolcano-touroperator.com/screening/ijen-screening-hotel-02.jpg Blood pressure check at JVTO office https://javavolcano-touroperator.com/screening/jvto-office-screening-1.JPG Oxygen saturation check at JVTO office https://javavolcano-touroperator.com/screening/jvto-office-screening-2.jpg Sample surat sehat (health clearance) printout https://javavolcano-touroperator.com/screening/print-surat-sehat-preview.png BBKSDA ticket terms — health certificate requirement https://javavolcano-touroperator.com/screening/bbksda/bbksda-ticket-terms-screenshot.jpeg Source: sources/ssot-image-asset-map health_screening group + uncertain group. Gas Masks — Separate from Screening Gas masks are provided by JVTO as a standard inclusion on all Ijen-relevant packages. This is independent of and separate from the health-screening process. Regardless of the mandatory health screening, gas masks are standard equipment on all JVTO Ijen routes. The hard gate No valid health certificate = no access to the crater zone. This is a BBKSDA rule. We will not take you up without it. Why each vital is measured Metric Why it matters Oxygen saturation (SpO₂) Baseline lung function before high-altitude sulfur exposure. Blood pressure Cardiovascular risk at 2,386 m (systolic / diastolic). Resting heart rate Cardiovascular baseline. Respiratory history Asthma or bronchitis — directly relevant to gas-mask use and sulfur exposure. Verify your physician Every JVTO surat sehat is issued by a named, individually auditable doctor — not an in-house printout. You can check the licence before you book. STR satusehat.kemkes.go.id KKI check kki.go.id/cekdokter What you should do before the trip → Disclose any pre-existing cardiovascular or respiratory condition in your inquiry form. → Bring any home-country medical paperwork relevant to altitude or respiratory conditions. → Get a good night of sleep before the screening session. → Avoid alcohol the night before — it can register as elevated blood pressure. Verify before you book You can check Dr. Irwandanu's licence at the Kemenkes SatuSehat and KKI registries linked above, and read the regulatory and police-safety context on the Police & Safety proof page . The certificate behind your climb is auditable — by design. Related Destination Ijen Crater → ◆ Quick Answers Ijen Health Screening: Common Questions Is Ijen health screening mandatory? A pre-hike health screening is included in your package and is mandatory for every guest before Kawah Ijen crater entry (supported by BBKSDA SE.1658/KSA.9/2024). It is conducted at your hotel before the guide briefing. What does the screening typically check? Typical checks include basic measurements such as blood pressure and oxygen level plus a short set of questions by trained medical staff, following local guidelines. What happens if someone is not cleared? If a guest is denied clearance, affected components may not operate for that person. Policy handling follows /policy/booking-payment-cancellation. Does screening guarantee nothing will happen? No. Screening reduces risk but conditions remain subject to local authority decisions, weather/visibility, and on-site safety assessments. How is screening-related data handled? If personal data is collected during screening, it is handled in line with JVTO privacy commitments and provider/authority requirements. See /policy/privacy. The principles are: layering for cold pre-dawn starts, grip for volcanic and canyon terrain, and waterproofing where you will get wet. Below is a destination-by-destination guide to what to bring, what the terrain demands, and what we provide. Mount Bromo Fitness level : Basic mobility. You step in and out of a 4WD jeep, walk short distances across uneven volcanic sand, and climb steps to the crater rim. No sustained uphill hiking is required. Suitable for most fitness levels, including children with basic mobility and older travellers who can handle short walks on uneven ground. What to bring: Warm layers — temperatures at the Penanjakan viewpoint run 5–15°C (41–59°F) pre-dawn Hat, gloves, and a scarf or buff Comfortable closed shoes (the Sea of Sand is dusty volcanic terrain; good grip recommended) A light jacket or windbreaker Small daypack — main luggage stays at the hotel during the sunrise sequence What JVTO provides: Private 4WD jeep (pre-arranged, included on all Bromo-relevant packages) Kawah Ijen Fitness level : Sustained uphill walk. The trail from Paltuding trailhead to the crater rim is approximately 3 km each way, taking around 1.5–2 hours to ascend on a steep, rocky path. Guests with heart, lung, or circulation conditions should consult their doctor before booking. This is a night hike — the midnight departure targets the Blue Fire viewing window; a pre-dawn (~03:00) departure is used if only sunrise is the target. What to bring: Warm layers for the midnight start — crater rim temperatures run 10–15°C (50–59°F) Long sleeves and full-length trousers Hiking shoes with good grip (the trail is dusty on the ascent and can be slippery on descent) A headlamp (JVTO provides headlamps on Ijen routes — bring your own as a backup) A spare scarf or dust mask for general dust (note: this is not a substitute for the JVTO-provided gas mask in the crater area) Silver jewellery warning : Do not wear silver on the Ijen hike. Sulphur gases tarnish silver and the reaction may be difficult or impossible to reverse. This applies to silver rings, bracelets, necklaces, earrings, and silver-coated watches. What JVTO provides: Professional gas mask (standard inclusion on all Ijen-relevant packages — separate from health-screening coordination) Headlamps Trekking poles Tumpak Sewu Fitness level : Balance and grip required. The canyon descent from the viewpoint platform to the waterfall base involves fixed ropes, wooden handholds, and steep, wet, slippery ground. There are river crossings to reach the base of the falls. This route is not recommended for guests with serious knee, ankle, or balance issues. What to bring: Clothing and shoes that can get completely wet and muddy — plan for it, not against it Sandals or water shoes with firm grip for river crossings (flat soles on river rocks are a slip hazard) A small towel and a full change of clothes for the return journey Waterproof bag or dry bag for valuables and electronics What JVTO provides: Guided canyon descent with briefing before departure Madakaripura Fitness level : Moderate — canyon wading and uneven terrain. The approach to Madakaripura involves wading through a narrow stream with wet stones underfoot. You will get wet in the canyon. The terrain is not technically demanding, but sure footing on slippery surfaces is important. What to bring: Waterproof bag — you will enter water and the canyon spray is heavy A full change of clothes and a towel Sandals or shoes that can get soaked and still grip wet rock Waterproof cases or dry bags for phones and cameras What is provided at the site: Helmets are provided at the canyon entrance by local site management (not a JVTO inclusion) Valuables — General Advice Leave jewellery (particularly silver, as noted above), extra cash, and valuables you cannot afford to damage or lose at the hotel when heading into volcanic or canyon environments. JVTO is not responsible for personal items lost or damaged on-site. What to bring: Warm layers — temperatures at the Penanjakan viewpoint run 5–15°C (41–59°F) pre-dawn Hat, gloves, and a scarf or buff Comfortable closed shoes (the Sea of Sand is dusty volcanic terrain; good grip recommended) A light jacket or windbreaker Small daypack — main luggage stays at the hotel during the sunrise sequence What JVTO provides: Private 4WD jeep (pre-arranged, included on all Bromo-relevant packages) Kawah Ijen Fitness level : Sustained uphill walk. The trail from Paltuding trailhead to the crater rim is approximately 3 km each way, taking around 1.5–2 hours to ascend on a steep, rocky path. Guests with heart, lung, or circulation conditions should consult their doctor before booking. This is a night hike — the midnight departure targets the Blue Fire viewing window; a pre-dawn (~03:00) departure is used if only sunrise is the target. What to bring: Warm layers for the midnight start — crater rim temperatures run 10–15°C (50–59°F) Long sleeves and full-length trousers Hiking shoes with good grip (the trail is dusty on the ascent and can be slippery on descent) A headlamp (JVTO provides headlamps on Ijen routes — bring your own as a backup) A spare scarf or dust mask for general dust (note: this is not a substitute for the JVTO-provided gas mask in the crater area) Silver jewellery warning : Do not wear silver on the Ijen hike. Sulphur gases tarnish silver and the reaction may be difficult or impossible to reverse. This applies to silver rings, bracelets, necklaces, earrings, and silver-coated watches. What JVTO provides: Professional gas mask (standard inclusion on all Ijen-relevant packages — separate from health-screening coordination) Headlamps Trekking poles Tumpak Sewu Fitness level : Balance and grip required. The canyon descent from the viewpoint platform to the waterfall base involves fixed ropes, wooden handholds, and steep, wet, slippery ground. There are river crossings to reach the base of the falls. This route is not recommended for guests with serious knee, ankle, or balance issues. What to bring: Clothing and shoes that can get completely wet and muddy — plan for it, not against it Sandals or water shoes with firm grip for river crossings (flat soles on river rocks are a slip hazard) A small towel and a full change of clothes for the return journey Waterproof bag or dry bag for valuables and electronics What JVTO provides: Guided canyon descent with briefing before departure Madakaripura Fitness level : Moderate — canyon wading and uneven terrain. The approach to Madakaripura involves wading through a narrow stream with wet stones underfoot. You will get wet in the canyon. The terrain is not technically demanding, but sure footing on slippery surfaces is important. What to bring: Waterproof bag — you will enter water and the canyon spray is heavy A full change of clothes and a towel Sandals or shoes that can get soaked and still grip wet rock Waterproof cases or dry bags for phones and cameras What is provided at the site: Helmets are provided at the canyon entrance by local site management (not a JVTO inclusion) Valuables — General Advice Leave jewellery (particularly silver, as noted above), extra cash, and valuables you cannot afford to damage or lose at the hotel when heading into volcanic or canyon environments. JVTO is not responsible for personal items lost or damaged on-site. It has run this way since March 2019 , for a volunteer conservation program called "Rijik" (Javanese for "tidy" / "clean"), during which park staff and volunteers descend into the crater area to remove an estimated 100–150 kg of trash accumulated from tourism and mining traffic. It is a small, easily-missed fact — most independent travelers and even some tour operators don't track it — but arriving on a Rijik day means being turned away at the gate after a 01:00 AM wake-up call and a night trek to the crater rim. JVTO checks this calendar before confirming any Ijen-inclusive itinerary, so it never becomes a guest's problem. What Is the Rijik Cleanup Program? Rijik is a scheduled ecosystem-cleaning day at TWA Ijen (the Ijen Nature Tourism Park). On the first Friday of every month, the park closes to tourism and mining traffic so park staff and community volunteers can clear trash from the crater rim, the descent trail, and the shoreline of the sulfur lake — waste that accumulates from the steady flow of tourists and traditional sulfur miners between cleanups. Each session typically collects an estimated 100–150 kg of trash . The program has run on this fixed monthly cadence since March 2019 , making it a predictable, recurring closure rather than an emergency or unplanned event. Why It Matters for Travelers Ijen night hikes are logistically unforgiving: guests are typically picked up from Bondowoso-area hotels around midnight to reach the crater rim in time for the blue-fire window before dawn. If a self-planned or unlicensed itinerary lands on a Rijik closure day, the outcome is a wasted pre-dawn wake-up and a turned-away group at the gate — with no advance warning, because the closure is a park operations detail, not something advertised on ticket-booking pages. No competitor operator publishes this fact in a dedicated guide. It is exactly the kind of operational detail that separates a licensed operator who tracks park administration from an itinerary assembled purely from generic travel-blog research. How JVTO Handles It Checked before confirmation. JVTO checks the TWA Ijen closure calendar before confirming any Ijen-inclusive itinerary against a guest's requested travel dates. Rerouted, not cancelled. If a preferred travel window falls on the first Friday of the month, JVTO reorders the itinerary — for example, visiting Bromo or Madakaripura first — so the Rijik closure day never disrupts a confirmed booking. This follows the same alternative-route approach used for PVMBG-driven closures; see Weather & Closures . Not the same as a safety closure. Rijik is a fixed conservation closure, unrelated to PVMBG (volcanology) alert-status closures, which are unscheduled and driven by real-time gas and seismic monitoring. Covered by the same cancellation terms. In the rare case a closure makes a program genuinely unworkable, the standard JVTO Lifetime Package Credit terms apply — see Booking, Payment & Cancellation Policy . ◆ Quick Answers Ijen Rijik Closure: Common Questions Why does Kawah Ijen close on the first Friday of every month? Since March 2019, TWA Ijen (the Ijen Nature Tourism Park) has closed to all visitors on the first Friday of every month for "Rijik" — a scheduled ecosystem-cleaning day. Park staff and volunteers descend into the crater area to remove trash left behind by tourism and mining traffic, typically collecting an estimated 100–150 kg of waste per session. It is a recurring conservation closure, not an emergency shutdown or a sign of a safety incident. Will my JVTO tour ever be cancelled because of the Rijik closure day? No. JVTO checks the TWA Ijen closure calendar before confirming any Ijen-inclusive itinerary and schedules guest departures to avoid the first Friday of the month. If a guest's preferred travel window happens to land on a Rijik closure day, JVTO adjusts the itinerary order in advance — for example, visiting Bromo or Madakaripura first — so the closure never disrupts a confirmed booking. Is the monthly Ijen closure the same as a PVMBG volcanic-activity closure? No, they are separate and unrelated. Rijik is a fixed, scheduled cleaning day that occurs on the first Friday of every month regardless of volcanic conditions. A PVMBG (Indonesian volcanology agency) closure is unscheduled and happens only when gas emissions or seismic activity cross an official safety threshold. JVTO monitors both: the fixed Rijik calendar for routine scheduling, and real-time PVMBG alerts for safety-driven closures. See Weather & Closures for how PVMBG-driven changes are handled. How much trash is removed during the Rijik cleanup at Ijen? Volunteers and park staff typically remove an estimated 100–150 kg of trash from the Kawah Ijen crater area during each monthly Rijik session — waste accumulated from tourism and mining traffic since the previous cleanup. When did the Ijen Rijik cleanup program start? The program has run since March 2019, with TWA Ijen closing to visitors on the first Friday of every month for the cleanup. JVTO has scheduled guest itineraries around this fixed closure day for the same period. Ready for operational certainty? That order shapes every operational decision we make. Safety at JVTO is not a marketing position — it is a written framework applied before and during every tour. We do not remove guests from real environments; we prepare them for those environments with accurate information, trained guides, proper equipment, and written contingency procedures. Guests consistently report pre-hike safety briefings as a defining feature of the JVTO experience. That is deliberate: every activity starts with a briefing because the alternative — assuming guests know what to expect — creates the conditions for preventable incidents. Plan-B Framework — Written Policy, Not a Promise When conditions change, JVTO does not improvise. We operate a documented Plan-B framework for volcanic closures, severe weather, and access restrictions. Before Day 1, we check road and park conditions, weather alerts, hotel and transport availability, and align with our local partners at each destination. If an alert or closure is issued — whether for volcanic activity at Bromo, gas conditions at Ijen, or flood risk at Madakaripura — we contact guests in advance, explain what has changed, and propose reasonable alternatives. During the tour, guides monitor weather, road conditions, crowding, and local announcements in real time. We may leave viewpoints earlier, arrive later, switch routes, or choose safer paths. If a key element of your package cannot operate — for example, if Bromo's national park closes due to volcanic activity — the policy response is documented in your booking: guests are briefed, alternatives are offered, and Package Credit is applied to unused portions where applicable. No guest is left without a program. That is the policy, written down. Safety Briefings Before Each Activity Before every hike, canyon descent, or jeep sequence, JVTO guides conduct a safety briefing. What to expect on the terrain, where to put your feet, when to hold the rope, what the gas mask covers and what it does not cover. Reviewers across multiple platforms name individual guides by name and cite these briefings specifically — Anjas, Taufik, Rendi, Gufron, Kiki. This pattern maps to what JVTO calls T4 in its review analysis: guests repeatedly mention feeling safe, well-informed, and prepared. The briefing is not optional and not abbreviated for speed. BBKSDA-Supervised Guide Training at Paltuding Ijen local guides at JVTO are HPWKI-affiliated (Himpunan Pelaku Wisata Khusus Ijen). HPWKI membership means completion of BBKSDA-supervised training — government-hosted, not self-certified. In May 2024, BBKSDA Jawa Timur ran a three-day training programme (20–22 May 2024) at Paltuding — the Ijen trailhead and visitor centre inside the park. The programme targeted 250 HPWKI-affiliated guides and covered: Conservation area awareness Local guide responsibilities within Kawah Ijen Natural Tourism Park SAR (Search and Rescue) techniques PPGD — Emergency Medical Response (Penanggulangan Penderita Gawat Darurat) This is the institutional training record for the guide team at Ijen. It was documented by BBKSDA Jawa Timur, not JVTO. The scope — SAR and emergency medical response — goes beyond standard guiding and positions guides as field extensions of park management. Gas Masks on Ijen Routes JVTO provides professional gas masks as a standard inclusion on all Ijen-relevant packages. Sulphur dioxide concentrations at the Ijen crater floor fluctuate with gas venting, wind direction, and access-point proximity. The masks are fitted, not optional accessories, and are briefed before the crater descent begins. A spare scarf or dust mask guests bring is not a substitute for the JVTO-provided gas mask in the crater area. Emergency Handling For serious medical situations on tour, JVTO guides coordinate with local clinics, evacuation services, and — where relevant — Ditpamobvit contacts in the park area. Because all tours are private, the guide and driver respond only to your group; there is no divided attention across strangers. JVTO strongly recommends that all guests carry valid travel insurance covering medical emergencies, evacuation, repatriation, trip interruption, and adventure activities including volcanic hiking and canyon descent. Insurance is not included in tour pricing. Guests under the influence of alcohol or substances may be refused participation in hikes, crater descents, or steep trails — this is a written safety policy, not a discretionary call. Routes and timings may be adjusted if conditions change. What safety support applies to Ijen routes? When Ijen is included, eligible routes typically include sulfur-rated gas masks, trekking support (as configured), and a mandatory pre-hike health screening arranged by JVTO. What should guests do to support safety? Be on time for pickups, follow on-site instructions, and disclose relevant health/fitness limitations before the tour where applicable. Are routes always accessible? No. Access can change due to weather, volcanic activity, or authority closures. See /travel-guide/weather-and-closures. What if something differs from the website text? When the volcanoes are off-limits, when the rains close the trails, and how JVTO reroutes without leaving you in a hotel for two days. Dry season Apr–Oct Wet season Nov–Mar Ijen closure 1st Friday monthly Authority BBKSDA / BBTNBTS / PVMBG Travel Guide Guide overview Ijen Health Screening Packing & Fitness Weather & Closures Safety on Tours Booking Information Police Escort for Groups FAQ Browse tours Reading time · 5 min Bromo and Ijen are active volcanoes. Tumpak Sewu and Madakaripura are canyon environments where rainfall matters. Conditions change. This page explains what we watch, how we respond, and what you can expect if your dates are affected. Mount Bromo — Closures & Seasonal Patterns Bromo sits inside the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park (BBTNBTS). When volcanic alert levels rise, park management or BNPB may restrict or close crater access, the caldera floor, or the national park roads. JVTO follows those instructions without exception. Volcanic closure SOP : If Bromo closes for volcanic activity during your booking window, JVTO activates its Plan-B framework — alternative viewpoints, rescheduled timing, or replacement destinations. Guests are briefed in advance. You will not arrive to find us improvising. Kasada festival : The annual Tengger Hindu ceremony at Pura Luhur Poten on the caldera floor falls on a date that varies by lunar calendar each year. During Kasada, Bromo crater access may be restricted or heavily crowded. JVTO activates its Plan-B SOP for bookings that coincide with this period. If your dates are near a Kasada window, ask us when you enquire. Best season for Bromo : Dry season, April–October. Pre-dawn temperatures at the Penanjakan viewpoint run 5–15°C (41–59°F). Main activities — sunrise at Penanjakan, the Sea of Sand jeep traverse, crater walk — happen in the pre-dawn window (03:00–05:00) before rain is more likely later in the day. Kawah Ijen — Gas Activity, Access Rules & Closures Ijen is monitored by BBKSDA East Java (bbksdajatim.org) and the Indonesian volcanology authority (PVMBG/Magma Indonesia). Several types of restriction apply: Monthly closure : The Ijen crater is closed to visitors on the first Friday of every month . This is a scheduled closure, not weather-dependent. If your Ijen hike falls on the first Friday of the month, JVTO will flag this when you enquire. Gas and safety closures : BBKSDA issues additional closures based on volcanic gas levels and safety assessments. These are announced via bbksdajatim.org. JVTO monitors these in real time and will not send guests to a closed crater. Blue Fire visibility : Blue Fire is a natural phenomenon subject to weather and gas activity. It is visible pre-dawn in suitable conditions at the crater floor. JVTO designs Ijen itineraries around a midnight departure to maximise the viewing window — but we cannot promise natural phenomena. Cloud cover, gas venting direction, and wind conditions are outside our control. Health certificate — mandatory : A recent local health certificate is mandatory for every guest before Kawah Ijen crater entry, per BBKSDA SE.1658/KSA.9/2024 (cited as supporting authority). JVTO coordinates the mandatory clinic workflow before the hike. No valid health certificate means no crater-zone access — this is a BBKSDA checkpoint requirement, not a JVTO policy. Best season for Ijen : Dry season, April–October. Crater rim temperatures run 10–15°C (50–59°F) at the midnight departure window. Tumpak Sewu & Madakaripura — Rainfall & Canyon Conditions Both Tumpak Sewu and Madakaripura are canyon and waterfall environments. Heavy rainfall can affect water levels, trail safety, and access. Tumpak Sewu : The canyon descent uses fixed ropes and handholds on steep, wet terrain. Heavy rainfall increases slip risk on the descent. Guides assess conditions on the day; if the route is unsafe, the guide makes the call. Madakaripura : The canyon approach requires wading through a stream. Water levels rise after heavy rain. The experience involves getting wet regardless of conditions — that is the nature of the site. Best season for both : Visiting during the dry season (April–October) is generally more comfortable, but these are year-round destinations. Even in the wet season, many Tumpak Sewu and Madakaripura days proceed without issue. Seasonal Overview — East Java Season Months Notes Dry season April – October Recommended for Bromo and Ijen. Clearer skies, lower rainfall, better road conditions. Wet season November – March Higher rainfall, possible cloud at viewpoints. Canyon destinations (Tumpak Sewu, Madakaripura) remain popular. Plan-B — What JVTO Does When Conditions Change If a key activity or destination is unavailable on your dates due to volcanic activity, official closure, or safety assessment: We contact you in advance — you are not surprised on the day. We explain what has changed and why. We propose reasonable alternatives: different viewpoints, adjusted timing, replacement destinations. If a key itinerary element cannot operate at all, Package Credit applies to the unused portion per your booking terms. JVTO does not bypass official restrictions. If BBKSDA, BBTNBTS, or BNPB closes a site, that closure applies to us regardless of your booking. For the full written policy on closures, reschedules, and Package Credit, see the Booking, Payment & Cancellation Policy . Routes may change due to volcanic activity, sulfur gas exposure levels, extreme weather/heavy rain, unsafe terrain, national park closures, or road/traffic constraints. Can blue fire or sunrise views be guaranteed? No. Visibility is natural-condition dependent and cannot be guaranteed. JVTO prioritizes safety and legal access. If a destination closes, what happens? JVTO may adjust timing, change viewpoints/segments, or substitute a safer alternative where feasible. Remedies follow the force majeure/change rules in /policy/booking-payment-cancellation. Do you operate during bad weather? Operations depend on safety and local conditions. If conditions are unsafe, the plan may be adjusted or stopped. What is the binding reference if there is a discrepancy? Your Official E-Voucher / Invoice (PDF) and the policy pages take precedence over non-binding summaries. Ready for operational certainty? We saw the gaps in safety standards first-hand and decided to build something different: private-only routes, realistic driving days, and clear written rules. Today, we act as a bridge between wild adventure and professional safety standards. How We Got Here 2015 — The Guesthouse Agung Sambuko — Mr. Sam — grew up in Bondowoso, the town closest to Kawah Ijen. In 2015 he opened the Ijen Bondowoso Homestay on Jl. Khairil Anwar No.102 (the current office address is No.102A — the 'A' suffix reflects the current office numbering), the same address where JVTO operates today. Booking.com guests rated the property 9.4 / 10 — an award that was shipped to the Bondowoso address that year. He was already an active officer in the Indonesian National Police, assigned to Ditpamobvit — the directorate responsible for security at vital tourist objects including the Ijen Crater area. Managing the guesthouse meant he saw both sides of East Java volcano tourism: the visitor experience and the operational safety gaps. Legal Formalization — PT Java Volcano Rendezvous The guesthouse era grew into PT Java Volcano Rendezvous, formalized with NIB 1102230032918 (TDUP issued 2023). Separately, Stefan Loose Reiseführer Indonesien: mit Reiseatlas (ISBN-13 9783770167654, p. 287) named "Agung" as the operator of the Ijen Bondowoso Homestay with tour arrangements — an independent German travel publisher, not a JVTO-authored reference, listing the same name at the same address. NIB 1102230032918 is the government-issued national business registration number, verifiable through Indonesia's OSS system. Why Private-Only The decision to operate private tours exclusively came from what Mr. Sam observed in the field: unlicensed operators running shared groups without consistent guides, no medical screening before Ijen hikes, casual attitudes toward BBKSDA permit requirements, drivers working routes they did not know. Private structure removes the coordination failures that come with mixed groups. Your vehicle and crew are assigned to your booking. Safety decisions are made for your group, not averaged across strangers with different fitness levels and objectives.
